precepts.text: In all Israel there was none so much praised as Absalom for his beauty, without blemish from the sole of his foot to the crown of his head. Beauty became his identity, and behind it came ambition, rebellion against his father, civil war, and death hanging by that very hair. Whenever physical attraction is in the forefront, the Bible shows trouble behind it.
precepts.point: Y'all take chess and spades seriously, seeing moves ahead and counting books, but not marriage. She looks good, I have to marry her so I can have her.

note.label: Marriage Beyond Romance: From Eden to Modern Confusion

precepts.why:
“But in all Israel there was none to be so much praised as Absalom for his beauty: from the sole of his foot even to the crown of his head there was no blemish in him.” Beauty became part of Absalom's identity. It was synonymous with him: his hair, his physical perfection.

And what came behind that? Ambition and rebellion. You get a big head about yourself and you start to believe certain things. Absalom rose up against his father, it came to civil war, and he died hanging from that very hair, the same thing that was vanity to him.

That is the same lesson as David on the roof in 2 Samuel 11:2. David saw a woman “very beautiful to look upon”, he saw her, he inquired, and he took her, the same pattern as Shechem with Dinah. Out of one fleeting moment of attraction came adultery, the murder of Uriah, a national scandal, the death of the child, and chaos in David's house the rest of his days. The Lord forgave him, but he left him with drama for moving that way. Then Absalom, celebrated for his own beauty, came to pride and rebellion.

Whenever physical attraction becomes the forefront of anything, the Bible shows you that trouble comes behind it. Y'all take chess and spades seriously, seeing moves ahead and counting books, but not marriage: she look good, I got to marry her so I can have her. Attraction is the gateway to destruction if that is the only thing you are moving on.

precepts.text: The revenger of blood himself shall slay the murderer; when he meeteth him, he shall slay him.
precepts.point: Joab had her act as a widow, saying the revenger of blood was coming for her last son. She knew, as Joab knew, that David was merciful, so she framed it around the law of the revenger of blood to draw out his mercy.
precepts.why:
“The revenger of blood himself shall slay the murderer: when he meeteth him, he shall slay him.”

That is the law the woman of Tekoah built her story on. Joab had her act as a widow whose two sons “strove together in the field, and there was none to part them, but the one smote the other, and slew him.” Now the whole family said, “Deliver him that smote his brother, that we may kill him, for the life of his brother whom he slew”. By that law they would slay her last son and “quench my coal which is left”, leaving her husband “neither name nor remainder upon the earth.”

She knew, as Joab knew, that David was merciful, so she framed it around the revenger of blood to draw out his mercy. She asked the king “that thou wouldest not suffer the revengers of blood to destroy any more, lest they destroy my son”, and David swore, “As the Lord liveth, there shall not one hair of thy son fall to the earth.”

note.label: Bishop Nathanyel | Revelation 1 A Visit From The Lord

precepts.why: We are still explaining the letters written to the angels over the seven churches, and that the saints shall judge the angels. “Then thine handmaid said, The word of my lord the king shall now be comfortable: for as an angel of God, so is my lord the king” See what she said about him: you are like an angel of God.

points: Joab the son of Zeruiah perceived that the king's heart was toward Absalom, and sent to Tekoah and fetched a wise woman, telling her to feign herself a mourner, put on mourning apparel, and speak to the king in the manner he taught her.
Joab put the words in her mouth. He set up the whole scene to move the king toward bringing Absalom home.

The woman of Tekoah told the king she was a widow whose two sons strove in the field, and one slew the other, and now the whole family rose up to kill the surviving son, seeking to quench her one remaining coal and leave her husband no name upon the earth. David swore that not one hair of her son would fall to the earth.

Joab had her act as a widow, saying the revenger of blood was coming for her last son. She knew, as Joab knew, that David was merciful, so she framed it around the law of the revenger of blood to draw out his mercy.

The woman then asked leave to speak one word, and turned it on David: why had he thought such a thing against the people of God, since by this judgment he condemned himself, in that he fetched not home his banished? We must needs die, as water spilt on the ground, yet God devises means that his banished be not expelled from him.

She turned his own words against him: you told me to bring my son back and nothing would happen to him, but what about your own son? Even the Most High is not a respecter of persons and does not keep his banished banished forever, so she trapped him in his own situation.

The king asked the woman not to hide the thing he would ask: was not the hand of Joab with her in all this? She answered that none could turn to the right hand or the left from what the king had spoken; his servant Joab bade her, and put all these words in her mouth. Joab did this to fetch about this form of speech, and the king was wise, according to the wisdom of an angel of God.

David knew. As anointed and worthy as David was, and as wise, there was no way he did not know what kind of man his own right-hand man Joab was. Though David made a mistake, the wisdom never departed from him; David was always on point. This also answers those who use David's mistake to justify their sins; they do not know the Bible, for his house had incest, murder, and now this scheme, and David still saw through all of it.

The king told Joab he had done this thing, and commanded him to go bring the young man Absalom again. Joab fell on his face, thanked the king, and said he now knew he had found grace in the king's sight. Joab went to Geshur and brought Absalom to Jerusalem, but the king said, Let him turn to his own house and not see my face.
Joab set the whole thing up to get Absalom back. David showed mercy by letting him return to Jerusalem, but said, Tell him not even to come see me; go to his own house.

In all Israel there was none so praised as Absalom for his beauty; from the sole of his foot to the crown of his head there was no blemish. When he polled his head at every year's end, because the hair was heavy on him, he weighed the hair at two hundred shekels after the king's weight. Unto Absalom were born three sons and one daughter named Tamar, a woman of a fair countenance.

Polled means to cut; people got haircuts back then. Two hundred shekels after the king's weight was heavy, for the king had pure everything, so that is a great deal of hair to grow back every year. Absalom named his daughter Tamar, which shows the respect he had for his sister.

Absalom was trying to get the king's attention, and when Joab would not respond, he set the man's field on fire to force the matter. This was straight craziness, but it finally brought him before the king, and David kissed him.

Absalom dwelt two full years in Jerusalem and saw not the king's face. He sent for Joab twice to send him to the king, but Joab would not come, so Absalom had his servants set Joab's barley field on fire. Then Joab came, and Absalom said, Let me see the king's face, and if there be any iniquity in me, let him kill me. Joab told the king, and Absalom came and bowed himself, and the king kissed Absalom.
